Crop for the square. Drag the photo inside the frame until the subject sits in the window, and use the zoom slider to tighten the crop. Faces and single objects work best; wide landscapes lose their horizon.

Instagram carousels work well with a set of instant prints that share one caption font and background; export each at Square or Portrait so the carousel does not jump in height. Etsy and print-on-demand listings convert better when the first image shows the print framed on a wall, which is exactly what the gallery frame plus the wall background produces. Portfolios and case studies benefit from the laptop and phone frames on a plain gradient, and the film strip is a quick way to present a series of three related shots in one image. Stories and Reels covers should use the Story size so nothing gets cropped by the app.
Pick a surface. The wall and desk backgrounds add a soft shadow and vignette, while transparent lets you drop the print onto your own design.
Tilt it a little. Two to six degrees is enough to suggest a print that was dropped on a desk. More than ten starts to feel like a scrapbook.

Write the caption by hand. Keep it short: a place, a date or a private joke. The casual font stack mimics marker on glossy paper; switch to serif for a more editorial look or mono for a lab-print feel.

Frame Lab is a static page. When you drop or paste a photo it is decoded into memory, drawn onto a canvas together with the frame and background, and encoded back to PNG or JPG by your browser. There is no upload endpoint and no server-side rendering, so family photos, unreleased product shots and client work never leave your computer. Your frame settings are saved in localStorage so the tool opens exactly how you left it.

Frame Lab may display advertisements served by Google AdSense to keep the tool free. Google and its partners may use cookies (including the DoubleClick cookie) to serve ads based on your prior visits to this and other websites. You can opt out of personalized advertising at Google Ads Settings or via aboutads.info. Visitors in the EEA and UK will be asked for consent where required.

Frame Lab renders every frame, device and background entirely inside your web browser using the HTML5 Canvas API. When you drop, pick or paste a photo it is decoded into your browser's memory, composed with the frame and background on a canvas, and encoded back to PNG or JPG on your device. No image, filename or pixel data is ever transmitted to our servers or to any third party. There is no upload endpoint. Closing or reloading the page clears the photos from memory.

If enabled, we use Google Analytics 4 to understand how the tool is used (page views, which frames and buttons are used, approximate region). Analytics never receives your photos or filenames. Google may set cookies or use similar technologies for this purpose. You can opt out with the Google Analytics opt-out add-on or by blocking analytics scripts.
